For eighty years the Saturday market in Fennick was held under one roof. The hall had been built in 1852 by public subscription, to bring the stalls in from out of doors, where they had stood in the rain on the open square, and the subscribers' names were cut into its oak beams. In February 1931 a gale tore away a third of its slates, and the rain came in again.

The town surveyor, Ida Merrin, found rot only in the gutters and the oak beams sound, but her report said the whole roof would have to be relaid. She set the repair at £500, warning that any delay risked a collapse under snow. The town already had £400 of debts on its new drains. Silas Ferrow, the grain merchant, offered £450 if the council would sell him the hall, and the mayor, Aldous Kerr, asked whether it might be cheaper to pull it down and rebuild.

It was Marta Quell, the cheese seller who spoke for the stallholders, who proposed moving the market to the open square. The hall held twenty-six stalls and the square had room for forty, and the stallholders, she said, would sooner pay for awnings than for mending a roof they meant to leave. The council agreed to her plan in one evening and kept Ferrow and his money waiting. On the first Saturday of April, handcarts carried the trestles down Bell Street, and the clerk, Ben Hollis, locked the hall behind them.

The square gave the market its forty stalls, and for three dry weeks the stallholders sold more than they ever had under the old roof.

Then came the first wet Saturday. By ten o'clock every trestle had been dragged in under the wide eaves of the locked hall, and the stallholders stood packed together out of the rain, much as their great-grandparents must have stood on the square in 1851. The eaves kept the market dry on wet Saturdays for six more years. It may be the only market ever to leave its hall to escape the rain and then shelter against its walls whenever the rain came.

The hall had been built in 1852 by public subscription, to bring the stalls in from out of doors, where they had stood in the rain on the open square, and the subscribers' names were cut into its oak beams. In February 1931 a gale tore away a third of its slates, and the rain came in again.

The town surveyor, Ida Merrin, found rot only in the gutters, and her report set the repair at £300. The town already had £400 of debts on its new drains. Silas Ferrow, the grain merchant, offered £450 if the council would sell him the hall, and proposed moving the market to the open square, which had room for forty stalls. Marta Quell, the cheese seller who spoke for the stallholders, offered that they would pay half the cost to mend the roof.

The council met eleven times that spring. The mayor, Aldous Kerr, favoured the sale; others backed the stallholders' plan; a few wanted the hall pulled down and rebuilt. The council could agree on nothing, and the clerk, Ben Hollis, entered each failed motion in the minutes. In October Merrin wrote again: the oak beams that carried the roof were sound, but the bare laths between them would collapse under a heavy snow.

The delay ran on into winter while the council waited for a majority. Ferrow withdrew his offer in November, and the stallholders' money, raised by then from more than two hundred names, was kept in the bank.

On the night of 9 January 1932, under eight inches of snow, the roof collapsed into the hall. That Saturday the market met inside the Corn Exchange. The minutes for the following week record the cost of clearing the site, which came to £41.

passage:
For sixty years the Ferrin loaf, a dark rye so coarse that the grain showed in every slice, had come from one oven in Tollin. Nell Ferrin had baked it first, and before she died she made her granddaughter Ada promise to keep it exactly as it was. It sat on the shelf by the window at four pennies. Orla Penn, the shop's oldest customer, bought one every morning, and Hob Tasker, the innkeeper, took two dozen a day for the Grey Hen, three dozen on Saturdays.

The rye was ground by Brann Cole, the miller below the town, and in October his great stone cracked. A new one could come from the quarry in spring. Until then Brann could grind only a finer flour on his small stone, though twenty sacks of coarse rye, about six weeks of loaves, stood already ground in his loft.

Joss, Ada's nephew and apprentice, carried Nell's old hand mill up from the cellar and tried it; grinding rye for a single batch took him the whole night. It was Ada's sister Merry, writing from Dunmere over the ridge, who suggested the answer: the big mill there sold coarse rye at a higher price, and the Tuesday carter would bring it across for a fee.

Ada wrote back the same day; a few pennies more seemed a small price for keeping her promise. When the first sacks came over the ridge, she stood at the counter to break the first loaf in two and study the crumb. It was right, and Orla said it tasted exactly as Nell's had. The loaf was on the shelf every morning that winter, but Ada chalked a new figure on the board by the door, and Hob grumbled as he paid.

The whole of Tollin's rye now came on one cart, over one high, bare road, and Brann's twenty sacks would cover six weeks at most if that road closed. By December Ada was at the shop window every Tuesday an hour before the cart could be due, watching the pass, and the deep snows that shut it most years were still to come.

She baked Brann's twenty sacks into a last six weeks of loaves and then took the rye loaf off the shelf until the new stone came. She had to break the news to Hob, who bought the Grey Hen's bread from a baker in Dunmere until spring. Through the winter the shop window held white loaves and wheat buns.

The new stone reached Brann's mill in the second week of April. He set it on a Monday, Ada baked Nell's loaf again on the Wednesday, and it went back on the board by the door at four pennies. Orla Penn bought the first one at a quarter past six and said it tasted as it always had.

Ada's sister Merry wrote that the big mill at Dunmere, over the ridge, sold coarse rye at a higher price. It was Joss who said what to do: if he and Ada took turns at the handle, the two of them could grind it all.

They used Brann's twenty sacks first, and in late November they began. Each night the two of them ground in turns, often still at the handle before the day could break, and the loaves reached the shelf hours later than they used to. Orla said they tasted exactly as Nell's had, and they were still sold at four pennies.

All winter the two of them fed the shop that way, through frost and short grey days. When the new stone came in spring, Ada could say what few bakers ever can: every loaf she had sold was the one she had promised Nell, kept so by two pairs of hands. It was hard, plain, faithful work, and Tollin ate the better for it.

Ada's sister Merry wrote that the big mill at Dunmere, over the ridge, sold coarse rye at a higher price. It was Hob Tasker who saw a way: baked only for the Saturday market, Brann's twenty sacks would last until spring.

Ada took the plan gladly, since it kept the loaf exactly as Nell had made it. From then on the rye loaf went into the oven on Friday nights alone, and on Saturdays the line for it ran out of the shop and across the square. It was still sold at four pennies, and Orla said it tasted exactly as Nell's had. By the first snows of winter the Saturday sales would regularly break ten dozen.

The one person in Tollin who suffered by the plan was the man who had thought of it. The Grey Hen's three dozen now had to be bought from the back of a queue that formed at dawn, and Hob spent his Saturday mornings stamping in the cold behind his own customers, while his cook asked daily how the clever idea was getting on.
